wine.name: Taylor's Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: A field blend of Douro red grapes: Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca at its core, with Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão and others.
wine.sites: Quinta de Vargellas in the Douro Superior, the backbone of the blend, with Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley and, since 2000, a little of Quinta do Junco beside it, all on steep terraced schist.
wine.making: Grapes from the house's own quintas are trodden by foot in lagares, the granite ones of Vargellas among them, and grape spirit is added partway through fermentation to stop it and keep the wine sweet. The wine then matures in wood for a little under two years, about twenty months for the 2017, before bottling; the rest of its life is spent in bottle.
wine.glass: Violet, blackberry and cassis over graphite and liquorice; sweet and dense, held by firm, grippy tannin and a long, dry edge. Old bottles turn to dried fig, cedar and leather.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed when young; a strong declared year wants twenty years or more in bottle and keeps for decades beyond.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand the bottle upright for a day, then decant it off its crust; a small wine glass.

label.means: Port of one declared year, approved by the IVDP and bottled young to age in bottle.
The protected name of Port, the fortified wine of the Douro, in Portuguese.
The name the house uses in some markets, the United States among them, for the same Port.

records.table: Founded in 1692, Taylor's treads by foot the grapes of its own quintas for its declared Vintage Port, with Vargellas in the Douro Superior as the backbone. Violet and blackberry sit on firm, grippy tannin; lay it down for decades, then decant it off its crust.
records.story: Taylor's dates its start to 1692, when an English merchant of the Bearsley family came to Portugal, trading at first in the lean red wine of the Minho rather than Port. In 1744 the house bought its first property in the Douro, near Régua, remembered in its First Estate Port. Partners joined through the nineteenth century, and the house says it took the name Taylor, Fladgate & Yeatman in 1844. Between 1893 and 1896 it bought the three properties of Vargellas in the Douro Superior, two of them from the contractor who had built the railway along the river, and joined them into one quinta. Phylloxera had ruined the vines; a partner of the Yeatman family rebuilt the estate, and by 1908, in the house's telling, its wine was good enough for the Vintage blend. In 1974, in a time of political turmoil in Portugal, Taylor's bought Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley, whose wine it had bought since the previous century. The house declares a Classic Vintage only in years it judges strong, announcing it by custom on 23 April of the second year; in other good years Vargellas is bottled alone. Taylor's means firm, slow Vintage Port, a wine for the long haul.

Taylor's and Taylor Fladgate are one house: the second name is the one the house uses in some markets, the United States among them.
Vintage Port spends under three years in wood and the rest of its life in bottle, so it throws a crust and must be decanted; a tawny does not.

report: Every fact rests on the house's own pages read through search summaries (Our History, the Vargellas winery, the Terra Feita purchase, Quinta do Junco, the 2017 Vintage Port, the Vargellas single quinta page); Wikipedia's Taylor, Fladgate and Yeatman page was read beside them for 1692 and 1744.

The year the partners joined differs between accounts (Joseph Taylor in 1814, 1816 or 1826; John Fladgate in 1836 or 1837; the name fixed in 1838 by one account and 1844 by the house's), so the story names no partner's year and gives the house's 1844 as its own account.

The founder and the Yeatman partner who rebuilt Vargellas are described, not named, as no dates for them were found in two sources; Junco's share in the blend since 2000 is on the house's Quinta do Junco page, which is not in the list for want of room.
The classification line rests on the IVDP's special categories pages, cited on the Graham's and Sandeman records of this group (https://www.ivdp.pt/en/wines/port-wines/special-categories/).
The library's region line has the first commercial LBV with the 1965 vintage released in 1970; it was not searched here and is left out of the record.
Living people met and kept out: the house's managing director and its head winemaker, both of the families that hold it; the read together agent may add their names to people.json.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, with 2 more on the IVDP's Vintage and tawny rules shared by the group.

wine.name: Graham's Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional at its heart, with Sousão and grapes from old mixed vines, in shares that change with each declared year.
wine.sites: Quinta dos Malvedos, the house's first vineyard, bought in 1890, high on the north bank of the Douro near Tua, where the Cima Corgo gives way to the Douro Superior, with Quinta do Tua, Quinta das Lages, Vila Velha and Vale de Malhadas, on the Douro's terraced schist.
wine.making: At the house's winery at Malvedos, robotic lagares built to copy the human foot, installed in 2000, tread the grapes, and grape spirit halts the fermentation. About two years in wood follow at the house's lodge of 1890 in Vila Nova de Gaia, where all its wines are aged, and the wine is bottled by the third year after the harvest, as the rules require.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, blackberry and violet over dark chocolate and liquorice, with a touch of eucalyptus; rich and sweet through the middle, gripped by firm, ripe tannin and long in the mouth.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to tempt young, but a strong year needs fifteen to twenty years to open and goes on for decades after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; after a spell standing upright, pour it off its crust into a decanter an hour or so before serving; small wine glasses.

label.means: The IVDP approved Port of a single declared year, in bottle by the third year after the harvest.
The Douro's fortified wine under its protected name, in Portuguese or in English.

records.table: At the heart of Graham's Vintage Port is Quinta dos Malvedos, bought in 1890 near Tua on the Douro's north bank by a house founded in 1820. Rich and plummy, it needs years in bottle and a decanter, and it is poured after dinner.
records.story: The Grahams were textile merchants, two brothers who in 1820, as the house tells it, accepted twenty seven barrels of Port in payment of a debt and so found themselves in the wine business. In 1882 a young Scot came out from Glasgow to work for the Grahams; his family, the Symingtons, became Port shippers in their own right. In 1890 the house bought its first vineyard, Quinta dos Malvedos, on a promontory above the Douro near Tua, and its vines became the cornerstone of Graham's Vintage Port; the lodge in Vila Nova de Gaia where the house ages its wines carries the same year in its name. In 1970 the young Scot's grandsons bought Graham's from the Graham family. The Vintage Port is made in the house's own winery at Malvedos, where robotic lagares built to copy the human foot have done the treading since 2000. A year the house judges strong becomes a declared Vintage; in a good year short of that mark, Malvedos goes into bottle under its own name. Among the Symington family's Vintage Ports, Graham's is the rich, plummy one.

others.name: Graham's Quinta dos Malvedos Vintage Port
others.note: Malvedos alone, bottled as a Vintage in good years the house leaves undeclared.

others.name: Graham's 20 Year Old Tawny
others.note: A blend of wines of many years aged in cask at the lodge of 1890, with the character of twenty years in wood.

others.note: A Reserve Ruby of the house, sold ready to drink.

traps: Quinta dos Malvedos on a label is a single quinta Vintage of an undeclared year, not Graham's declared Vintage Port.
Graham's was founded by the Graham brothers in 1820 and bought by the Symington family only in 1970, though a Symington first worked for the house in 1882.
Six Grapes is a Reserve Ruby ready to drink, not a Vintage Port.

wine.name: Quinta do Noval Nacional Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: A field blend of many Douro varieties planted together, among them Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinto Cão, Tinta Roriz and Sousão, every vine on its own ungrafted roots.
wine.sites: The Nacional parcel, a small plot at the heart of the Noval vineyard on the terraced schist above Pinhão. Its vines stand on their own roots rather than American rootstock and are replanted the same way, so they are not pre-phylloxera survivors.
wine.making: Foot treading in the quinta's granite lagares, exactly as for the rest of the Noval vineyard, comes first, and a dose of grape spirit cuts the fermentation short. The wine is then held for about eighteen months in large casks of oak and chestnut in the estate's temperature controlled cellars in the Douro before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, violet and blackberry, with liquorice and dark chocolate beneath, deeper and denser than the estate's other Vintage Port; sweet yet gripped by tight, firm tannin. With age it moves towards dried fig, cedar and tobacco.
wine.ageing: Slower to open than Noval's own Vintage Port; the house gives it a drinking window of five to a hundred years after bottling, and strong years are kept for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a day upright, then a gentle decanting off the crust shortly before serving; a small glass for wine.

label.means: The ungrafted parcel inside Quinta do Noval; the house reads the name as Portuguese vines in Portuguese soil.
A wine estate in Portugal; here the Noval estate above Pinhão.
A declared year's Port, bottled young so that it ages in the bottle; Nacional is declared apart.

records.table: Quinta do Noval Nacional is a Vintage Port from a small parcel of ungrafted vines at the heart of the Noval estate above Pinhão, trodden by foot and declared only when the house judges a year worthy of it. It is dense and slow to open.
records.story: The name Noval first appears in the land registers in 1715. Phylloxera left the vineyard in ruins; in 1894 a Port shipper bought the estate and replanted it, and his son in law went on to widen its narrow old terraces so that the vines could make better use of the land and the sun. Inside the vineyard a small plot was planted on its own roots, ungrafted; the house says its name, Nacional, means Portuguese vines in Portuguese soil, with no foreign rootstock. Noval made its name in 1931, on the house's own word, by declaring both a Vintage Port and a Nacional in a year when most shippers did not, with the world in depression and the large 1927 vintage unsold. In 1981 a fire destroyed the house's lodge, offices and records in Vila Nova de Gaia, and the stocks were later moved to a temperature controlled cellar on the quinta. The family that had held Noval since 1894 sold it in 1993, and it joined AXA Millésimes. Nacional is declared on its own judgement: in 1996 it was declared when Noval was not, and in 2007 Noval was declared without it. Nacional shows the Douro what ungrafted vines can give.

others.name: Quinta do Noval Vintage Port
others.note: The estate's Vintage from the rest of the vineyard, declared on its own judgement apart from the Nacional.

others.name: Quinta do Noval Colheita

traps: Nacional is a parcel inside Quinta do Noval, not a separate quinta, and it is declared apart from Noval's own Vintage Port.
Ungrafted is not pre-phylloxera: the Nacional vines grow on their own roots and are replanted that way.
Nacional names the ungrafted parcel, not the grape Touriga Nacional; the wine is a field blend.

wine.name: Barca Velha
wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional at its heart, with Tinta Roriz and other Douro grapes; the shares change with each declared year.
wine.sites: Quinta da Leda in the Douro Superior gives the greater part, with grapes from other vineyards at several altitudes in the same subregion; the first vintages were made at Quinta do Vale Meão, a Ferreira family estate there.
wine.making: The wine is aged for about a year and a half in French oak barrels, most of them new, then rests for years in bottle while the house watches it. Only then does the winemaking team decide whether the year is Barca Velha or Reserva Especial, so a vintage reaches the market eight or nine years after the harvest.
wine.glass: Cedar and cigar box over blackcurrant, sour cherry and plum; savoury and restrained rather than ripe, with fine, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Released when the house judges it ready to begin drinking, eight or nine years after the harvest, it goes on gaining for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an hour ahead, an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Old boat in Portuguese; the name is printed only in declared years.
The appellation of the valley's unfortified wines; Port carries the separate name Porto.
The house name of Ferreira's unfortified Douro wines, after Dona Antónia Ferreira's nickname.

records.table: Barca Velha is Casa Ferreirinha's unfortified Douro red, first made in 1952 and released after long rest in bottle, only in years its makers think fit to bear the name. Savoury, cedar framed and fresh, it showed that Port's grapes could make a dry red to keep.
records.story: Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira (1811 to 1896), widowed at thirty three, took charge of the Ferreira house, founded in 1751, and added estate after estate in the Douro; her countrymen called her Ferreirinha, little Ferreira. The dry wine that carries her nickname began more than half a century after her death. Fernando Nicolau de Almeida (1913 to 1998), whose father was the house's technical director, wanted a Douro red made with the care given to Vintage Port. At Quinta do Vale Meão, in the heat of the Douro Superior, he cooled the fermenting wine with ice brought by lorry from Matosinhos, near Porto, and in 1952 declared his first Barca Velha, selling it only in 1960, when he judged it ready to begin drinking. The harvest of 1960 gave the first Reserva Especial, the name for strong years judged short of Barca Velha. The Ferreira house joined Sogrape in 1987, and in later decades Quinta da Leda in the Douro Superior became the main source of the blend. The 2015, released after nine years, was the twenty first Barca Velha since 1952. It marks where the Douro's fine dry reds begin.

others.name: Casa Ferreirinha Reserva Especial
others.note: From strong years the team judges closer to Reserva Especial than Barca Velha; first made in 1960.

others.name: Quinta da Leda
others.note: The single estate red of the Douro Superior quinta that gives most of Barca Velha.

traps: Barca Velha is not made every year: strong years that fall short may be released as Reserva Especial, and many years give neither.
Ferreirinha is the nickname of Dona Antónia Ferreira, a person, not a place.
Barca Velha is an unfortified red of the Douro DOC, not a Port, though it comes from the same grapes.

report: Fernando Nicolau de Almeida's dates, his father's post, Vale Meão, the ice from Matosinhos and the release of the 1952 in 1960 rest on Wikipedia and Observador's special on Barca Velha (https://observador.pt/especiais/barca-velha-ou-a-historia-de-como-nascem-os-grandes-vinhos/), with Infopédia agreeing on the dates; Observador is left out of sources for want of room.
The purpose of the ice, to cool the fermentation in the heat, is implied rather than stated, as the summaries read did not say it in so many words.
The barrel time rests on two release notes (sixteen months in new French oak for the 2008, eighteen months mostly new for the 2015); early vintages saw Portuguese oak by one account only, left out.

The library gives the grapes as led by Tinta Roriz and Touriga Franca; Sogrape names Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional first, and one account has Tinta Roriz dominant in early years such as 1982 and Sousão added in 2015, so the record gives the two Tourigas at the heart and Tinta Roriz beside them.

The founding year 1751 is the Ferreira house's, as Sogrape gives it; Casa Ferreirinha is the name of its unfortified wines, and no source read dated that name. The year 1987 for Sogrape rests on Sogrape's own article on the Porto Ferreira Vintage 2018.
The meaning of the name Barca Velha beyond its translation, old boat, was given by one source only (sailing boats that carried young Port downriver) and is left out.

wine.name: Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny Port
wine.classification: Tawny with an indication of age, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP
wine.grapes: A blend of Douro red grapes: Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinta Amarela and Tinto Cão.
wine.sites: Grapes from vineyards along the Douro, blended and aged downriver in the house's lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented on their skins until grape spirit is added to stop the fermentation and keep the sugar. The wines then age for many years in oak casks in the house's lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia, and wines of several ages are blended to show the character of twenty years in wood.
wine.glass: Amber with a red edge; walnut, toasted almond, dried fig and orange peel over caramel and a hint of cinnamon, sweet and silky, lifted by fresh acidity; the nutty finish lingers.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when bottled and made to be drunk rather than laid down: its ageing is done in cask, and it throws no crust.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, lightly chilled; it needs no decanter; a white wine glass of modest size.

label.means: An indication of age: the blend shows the character of twenty years in cask, not the age of every wine.
Port aged in wood until its colour fades towards amber and its fruit turns to nuts and caramel.
Port's protected name in Portuguese; an aged tawny's label also gives its bottling year.

records.table: Under the caped Don of a house founded in London in 1790, Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny is Port aged for many years in oak casks in its lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia. Walnut, orange peel and caramel; pour it lightly chilled, straight from the bottle.
records.story: The Don, the caped silhouette of Sandeman, is younger than the house: an artist at a printing firm drew him in 1928, in the black cape of a Portuguese student and a Spanish hat, one for Port and one for sherry. The house itself began in 1790, when a Scot of the Sandeman family, twenty five years old and the son of a cabinetmaker, borrowed from his father to set up as a wine merchant in London. From the start the house dealt in Port and sherry, the two fortified wines of Iberia, and at first it traded not from offices of its own but from Tom's Coffee House in Birchin Lane, as merchants then did. The house recalls that the founder bought lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia to hold its Port before shipment, and by the middle of the nineteenth century it was shipping fine old tawny aged in its cellars. In 1952 the firm became a public company; Seagram took it over in 1979 or 1980, as accounts differ, and in 2002 it joined Sogrape, the Portuguese wine group. The 20 Year Old shows what decades in cask do to Port: fruit turned to walnut, orange peel and caramel, poured cool and without a decanter.

traps: Twenty years on a tawny label is an indication of age, the character of the blend, not the age of every wine in it.
Sandeman was founded in London by a Scot, not in Porto; its Port ages in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia across the river.
Decanting is for Vintage Port, which leaves a crust in the bottle; a 20 Year Old Tawny did its ageing in cask and leaves none.

opts: No: the blend shows twenty years' character

questions.exp: An indication of age describes the character of a blend of wines of several ages aged in wood; a tawny from a single harvest would be a Colheita, not a 20 Year Old.

questions.q: The Sandeman Don, the caped silhouette on the label, was first drawn in which year?
questions.exp: The Don was drawn in 1928 at a printer's studio; 1790 is the founding in London, and 1952 the year the family firm became a public company.

report: The house's history, the Don and the 20 Year Old's making and service rest on Sandeman's own pages read through search summaries; the one fetch of sandeman.com was refused and not retried.

The founder is described rather than named: his birth in 1765 follows from the house's page (twenty five in 1790) and a wine glossary, but his death in 1841 was in one source only; Perth as his home is in a partner's page and a Wikipedia mirror, so the story leaves it out.

Seagram's purchase is 1980 by the house's page and 1979 by Wikipedia; the story keeps 1980 as the house's account. The house's page calls the change of 1952 becoming a public company; one glossary says a stock corporation.
The grapes rest on the house's sheet hosted by Grape to Glass, with the IWSC entry agreeing (it names Trincadeira, another name for Tinta Amarela); neither gives a share the record repeats.
The house's sheet advises 12 to 16 degrees Celsius; the Codex's service quiz gives 12 to 14 for a 20 Year tawny, and the record keeps 12 to 14, inside both.
Quinta do Seixo in the Cima Corgo, between Régua and Pinhão on the south bank, is Sogrape's own account (https://sogrape.com/tourism/quinta-do-seixo), with a merchant's page agreeing.
The pick stands: Sandeman's best known everyday Port is a Reserve Ruby, but the 20 Year Old is its aged tawny of record and the Don's house is known for tawny; no swap is proposed.

Living people met and kept out: the seventh generation member of the family who shares the founder's name. Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, with the IVDP's tawny rules shared by the group, and one refused fetch.

changed: wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz above all is now the five grapes listed without a share, as the importer's sheet and the IWC entry give them without one.

wine.making: hand picked, destemmed and crushed and a controlled temperature are cut, resting only on the house's sheet as a merchant hosts it; the record keeps the fermentation stopped by grape spirit and the years in oak at Gaia.
wine.ageing: the house's advice to finish an opened bottle within two or three months is cut for the same reason; it now says the ageing is done in cask and the wine throws no crust.
wine.serve: though a little air helps is cut, in no source of this check.
story: the founder's lodges at Gaia and the old tawny of the mid nineteenth century are both told as the house's account, as its history page gives them; cool cellars is now its cellars.

story: the family ran the firm until 1952 is cut, since outside accounts have it a family business until Seagram; Seagram's purchase is now 1979 or 1980, as accounts differ, where the record kept the house's 1980 alone.
open: The bottling year on an aged tawny's label rests on secondary accounts and the house's own page naming its bottling; the IVDP pages read here state it plainly only for the special categories with a harvest year.
